title: Multi-tenant architecture, tenant unit and isolation profiles
status_rationale: Requirements define three isolation profiles (A shared database with per-tenant schema, B dedicated database on shared platform, C dedicated infrastructure) in UNB-TEN-002. CNV-TEN-001 makes the legal sponsor the tenant unit, with partner and program isolation inside the sponsor cell by typed partitioning and negative tests. CNV-ARC-001 places the ledger in one managed PostgreSQL cluster with a schema and database role per sponsor and row-level security on every tenant table. No database is selected or deployed; nothing is implemented.
target_answer: Unbound's tenant unit is the legal sponsor. Each sponsor is a cell: by default a dedicated schema and database role in a shared managed PostgreSQL cluster (profile A), with dedicated database (B) or dedicated infrastructure (C) available when risk or contract requires; business logic does not fork by profile. Inside a cell, distribution partners and programs are separated by typed partitioning in code, row-level security in the database, and negative tests. Isolation never relies on a tenant_id filter in application code alone. Shared services (identity, charity reference registry, orchestration, telemetry, model services) are listed in a SharedStoreRegister with permitted fields and classification; donor and advisor personal data never enters a shared store except as a keyed token. The isolation profile and controls in effect for each tenant at any time are recorded as append-only events.
current_practice: Not implemented. Requirements and an architecture specification exist (unbound@9b38de47:requirements/PARTNER-SEGREGATION-AND-TENANCY.md; unbound@9b38de47:architecture/TENANT-AWARE-PERSISTENCE-DESIGN.md), explicitly not implemented or validated.
intended_practice: Resolve the open architecture decisions (database engine and provider, key hierarchy, row-level security role), then build the sponsor cell model.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design isolates each sponsoring organization in its own database schema and role by default, with dedicated database or infrastructure options, and separates partners within a sponsor by typed code, database row-level security and negative tests. This is designed, not built or tested.
residual_risks: Shared-cluster profile A shares the database engine, administrators, extensions and catalog; a database engine vulnerability or superuser compromise crosses all sponsor cells on that cluster.
open_questions: Reconcile CNV-ARC-001 (row-level security on every tenant table in a schema-per-sponsor cluster) with PARTNER-SEGREGATION-AND-TENANCY.md, which states a shared-schema row-level-security model is not approved as a default profile. The likely reading is that RLS is defense in depth inside a sponsor schema, not the tenant boundary; this should be stated explicitly.
Which managed PostgreSQL provider and which major version will host the shared cluster, given Strata currently supports only PostgreSQL 16?

title: Tenant context derivation, routing and connection hygiene
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-004 refined by RR-UNB-TEN-004-r1 requires the TenantConnectionBroker to derive tenant from the authenticated principal's server-held entitlements, accept only server-issued opaque selection tokens, revalidate on every request and ignore client-supplied schema, database, host or tenant identifiers. The persistence design requires resetting session authorization and search path before pooling. UNB-TEN-003 covers background jobs and agent paths. Not implemented.
target_answer: The tenant for every request, job and message is derived from the authenticated principal's server-held entitlement set; a user entitled to several tenants selects one through an opaque, server-issued, session-bound token that is revalidated on every request. Headers, parameters, subdomains, schema hints and partner API fields cannot select a tenant. The connection broker binds an allowlisted schema and tenant-specific database role per transaction, never interpolates identifiers, never relies on a mutable default search path, and resets role, session settings and search path before returning a connection to the pool. Background jobs and message consumers carry a signed tenant context in the message envelope and open tenant-bound units of work; there is no cross-tenant job identity except governed platform maintenance under break-glass rules.
current_practice: Not implemented. Requirements exist with acceptance criteria.
intended_practice: Implement the broker and pooled-connection reset with negative tests (spoofed tenant, pooled leakage).
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design determines the tenant only from the verified user's server-held entitlements, ignores any tenant hints sent by clients or partners, and resets database session state before connections are reused. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: A defect in the broker affects every tenant; it is a single point of failure that needs independent testing.

title: Tenant isolation by construction: verified tenant context as a required type
status_rationale: The tenant-aware persistence design proposes F# contracts in which VerifiedTenantContext has a private constructor produced only by a trusted resolver, and the only way to open a unit of work takes that context; connection strings and schema names are omitted from application callers. The design states these contracts are illustrative and not compiled. SEC-DB-001 requires all database access through Strata, but the current-state brief finds no verified runtime typed query interface in Strata. Nothing is implemented.
target_answer: Application code cannot obtain a database connection or issue a query without a VerifiedTenantContext value, and that value can be constructed only by the trusted tenant resolver after authentication and entitlement checks. All repository and query functions take the context as a required parameter and bind tenant schema and role from it, so a query that spans tenants or omits the tenant cannot be written in application code and fails to compile. Within a sponsor cell, partner and program scope are typed the same way. The guarantee is scoped and stated: it covers application command and query code in the governed modules; it does not cover migrations, platform maintenance, break-glass, the database engine itself, or code that uses reflection or unsafe interop, each of which is controlled separately (Strata-declared grants and RLS, break-glass rules, SEC-EXEC-001 and SEC-LANG-001 analysis). Build provenance links the deployed binary to the checked source, and database-level enforcement remains as an independent second layer.
current_practice: Not implemented; illustrative design only. The enabling typed data access component is not identified (Strata provides schema management, not runtime queries).
intended_practice: Build the tenant-bound unit-of-work and query layer, prohibit raw connections in governed modules by analyzer, and keep database roles and RLS as an independent layer.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design aims to make cross-tenant queries impossible to write in application code by requiring a verified tenant context that only the platform's tenant resolver can create, with database-level controls as a second layer. This is an architectural design; it is not built or tested, and the guarantee will be stated with its exact scope.
residual_risks: F# private constructors and union cases can be bypassed through .NET reflection or unchecked default values; the guarantee depends on enforced prohibitions.
A correct type can carry a wrong tenant if the resolver itself is wrong.
Database-side paths (SECURITY DEFINER functions, views, triggers) are outside the type system.
open_questions: Which component implements the typed, tenant-bound query layer assumed by SEC-DB-001 and the persistence design?

challenge.customer_intent: Be certain that our donors' and clients' data can never be returned to another sponsor or partner.
challenge.adverse_outcome: A cross-tenant data leak, the most damaging and reputationally fatal failure for a multi-tenant financial platform.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Conventional assurance is tenant_id filters in application code plus periodic cross-tenant penetration testing; a single forgotten filter leaks data and tests sample only some paths.
challenge.legally_required: No statute prescribes the technique; GLBA, Regulation S-P and state privacy laws require safeguards and impose breach consequences.
challenge.contractually_required: Bank and wealth-manager contracts commonly require logical segregation and annual penetration tests that include tenant isolation.
challenge.historical_convention: Shared schema with tenant_id plus pen test; or dedicated instances for large customers.
challenge.architectural_elimination: The 'forgot the tenant filter' defect is eliminated in scope: application code that lacks a VerifiedTenantContext cannot reach the database. Out of scope: migrations, maintenance, break-glass, engine bugs, reflection and unsafe code, and wrong resolver logic.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Compiler plus analyzers that forbid raw connections, reflection and unsafe code in governed modules; database roles and RLS independently.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Each build yields analyzer results proving no raw connection usage in governed modules, plus generated cross-tenant negative tests.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Type-level tenant binding plus per-sponsor schema and role plus RLS plus continuous cross-tenant probes, with independent penetration testing focused on the out-of-scope paths and the resolver.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Partially by a technical reviewer with F# expertise who can inspect the context type, the resolver and the analyzer rules; most bank assessors cannot evaluate a type-system argument and will rely on independent testing and build provenance.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: A bank CISO is likely to regard the design as a genuine strength and a differentiator in architecture review, but unlikely to accept it instead of independent cross-tenant penetration testing and conventional segregation evidence. Reasons: examiners expect independent testing under interagency third-party guidance; the claim is about source code while the risk is in the running system; the guarantee has exclusions; and the bank's own reviewers may not be able to verify it. Acceptance improves if an independent firm reviews the construction and its scope and the claim is backed by build provenance and continuous probes.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Any governed module able to open a raw connection; reflection or unsafe code permitted; a resolver defect; shared caches or indexes outside the typed path; the absence of the typed query component altogether.
challenge.conventional_cost: Annual penetration tests and remediation; risk of undetected regressions between tests.
challenge.alternative_cost: High upfront engineering for the typed data layer and analyzers; penetration testing still required.
challenge.alternative_risks: Overstating the guarantee in sales materials; reviewers dismissing it as marketing if scope is not explicit.
supporting_arguments: Moves isolation from thousands of call sites to one constructor and one resolver.
Compile-time failure is earlier and cheaper than test or pen-test discovery.
Layered with database-level enforcement, a single failure does not leak data.
opposing_arguments: The enabling component does not exist yet.
Type-system guarantees are routinely bypassable in .NET through reflection unless prohibited and checked.
Institutions are required to obtain independent assurance and cannot rely on vendor reasoning.
Many real cross-tenant leaks occur in caches, search indexes, logs and AI context, outside the relational path the type protects.

title: Database-enforced tenant separation: roles, schema privileges, row-level security and catalog exposure
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-005 requires partner roles unable to read or write other schemas and threat modeling and negative tests for search paths, SECURITY DEFINER routines, migrations, pooling, shared extensions and administrative credentials. CNV-ARC-001 requires RLS on every tenant table. Strata (pilot) declares and compares grants and RLS policies, enables and forces RLS when declared, and discloses when RLS is not forced (table owner bypass). Strata research recorded that PostgreSQL catalog metadata is visible to roles without schema USAGE (EV-STRATA-2026-E7A9). Nothing is deployed.
target_answer: Each sponsor cell has its own schema and database roles; tenant roles have no privileges on other cells' schemas and none are granted to PUBLIC. Every tenant table in a cell has row-level security enabled and forced, so table owners cannot bypass it, with policies keyed to partner and program scope; no application role has BYPASSRLS or superuser. Grants and policies are declared in Strata and checked before each deployment, and a release check fails if any tenant table lacks enabled and forced RLS or if any tenant role holds privileges outside its cell. SECURITY DEFINER routines are prohibited in tenant schemas unless reviewed with a pinned search path. Because PostgreSQL system catalogs are readable across schemas and some catalogs (roles, databases) are cluster-wide, schema, role and object names contain no customer-identifying information, and customers needing metadata confidentiality use the dedicated-database profile.
current_practice: Not deployed. Strata (strata@c6a384ec) can declare grants, RLS policies and ENABLE or FORCE settings and reports drift; it has invariants noGrantsToPublic, everyTableHasAPrimaryKey and everyForeignKeyIsIndexed, but no invariant that every tenant table has forced RLS. Strata documents that a grantee the project never names is untouched, so privileges of undeclared roles are not reported by default.
intended_practice: Add Strata invariants (or a separate check) for forced RLS on tenant tables and for cell-confined grants; adopt opaque naming; test UNB-TEN-005 scenarios.
provable: Strata source and its catalog-visibility evidence record can be shown as tool capability and research. Nothing about an Unbound database.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design has the database itself enforce separation through per-sponsor schemas and roles and forced row-level security, checked before each deployment by Echelon's Strata tool. This is designed; no production database exists.
residual_risks: Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass RLS; these are break-glass only.
RLS has documented side channels (for example constraint and foreign key checks can reveal row existence); it is defense in depth, not the sole boundary.
Cluster-wide catalogs reveal role and database names to any connected role.

challenge.customer_intent: Have the database refuse cross-tenant access even if the application is wrong.
challenge.adverse_outcome: An application defect or injection returns another tenant's rows.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Database-level separation is strong when correctly configured, but RLS and grants are frequently misconfigured (policies not forced, owners bypassing, permissive defaults) and drift silently.
challenge.contractually_required: Logical segregation is commonly required; the mechanism is rarely specified.
challenge.historical_convention: Separate databases for large customers; tenant_id columns for others; RLS increasingly common.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Not eliminated; reduced. Cross-schema access by tenant roles is eliminated by privilege design in scope; owner bypass of RLS is eliminated by FORCE.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Strata pre-deploy comparison plus a release check for forced RLS and cell-confined grants (the latter not yet present in Strata).
challenge.continuous_evidence: Per-deployment Strata diff with explicit not-compared and unverifiable states.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Dedicated database per sponsor for those requiring it; opaque naming for shared clusters.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes; grants and policies are inspectable, and negative tests can be run by assessors.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely; database-level segregation is familiar to bank assessors.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Application connecting as table owner without FORCE; BYPASSRLS on application roles; SECURITY DEFINER routines with mutable search path.
challenge.alternative_cost: Higher per-tenant infrastructure for dedicated profiles.
challenge.alternative_risks: Many schemas in one cluster stress migrations and planning; UNB-TEN-018 requires benchmarking first.
supporting_arguments: Strata's honest coverage reporting addresses silent drift.
opposing_arguments: Catalog metadata visibility across schemas is a real confidentiality gap in shared clusters.
Strata is pilot and lacks a forced-RLS invariant today.

title: Cross-tenant isolation testing and continuous verification
status_rationale: The tenant-aware persistence design defines a test matrix per profile (cross-tenant SQL access denied, spoofed routing denied, pooled connection leakage, AI retrieval and telemetry isolation, noisy neighbor). PARTNER-SEGREGATION lists 14 adversarial scenarios. AUTH-T05 requires cross-tenant requests denied, alerted and evidenced. No tests exist; no penetration test has been performed.
target_answer: Every build runs the full isolation test matrix for each supported profile against real PostgreSQL: cross-tenant reads and writes, spoofed routing hints, pooled connection reuse, background job context, cache and index isolation, and AI retrieval. In production, synthetic canary tenants continuously attempt cross-tenant access through public interfaces and every denial is recorded and alerted. An independent penetration test focused on tenant isolation is performed before production and annually, and customers may test isolation themselves using two provisioned test tenants under agreed rules.
intended_practice: Build the matrix with the persistence layer; commission independent testing before production.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet built or tested Unbound's tenant isolation. Automated cross-tenant tests on every build, continuous production probes and independent testing before production are planned.
residual_risks: Tests encode known paths; novel paths (new caches, new AI features) need the release check that every new store is in the isolation map.

challenge.customer_intent: Obtain proof, not promises, that tenants are isolated.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Isolation regressions introduced between annual tests.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Annual cross-tenant penetration tests are valuable but sample one point in time and depend on scope and tester access to two tenants.
challenge.legally_required: No statute requires it of the vendor.
challenge.contractually_required: Commonly required by banks: annual independent pen test including multi-tenant testing.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Release blocked on any isolation test failure.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Per-build matrix results; production canary denial telemetry.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Continuous automated testing plus production canaries plus independent testing.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes; results and canary telemetry can be shared, and customers can test directly.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Customers will value continuous evidence and customer-run testing, but will not drop the independent test requirement.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If tests run only against mocks rather than real database roles and policies.
challenge.alternative_cost: Engineering plus canary operation; independent tests still needed.
challenge.alternative_risks: Canary probes could themselves create noise or false alarms.
supporting_arguments: Every release is tested on the exact isolation paths.
opposing_arguments: First-party tests are not independent assurance.

title: Isolation beyond the database: caches, queues, search, files, logs, backups and AI context
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-009 extends isolation to caches, queues, event streams, outboxes, object storage, search indexes, backups, logs, observability, prompt and context construction, embeddings, evaluation datasets and generated documents. UNB-RCN-PLT-004 requires AI context to be retrieved through the public query layer under the initiating principal's VerifiedTenantContext with retrieved resource IDs logged. UNB-TEN-014 requires tenant-aware backup and restore with documented limitations. MON-014 requires redaction in monitoring. Not implemented.
target_answer: Every secondary store is listed in the isolation map with its tenant key: cache keys and queue topics are tenant-prefixed by the same typed context; search and vector indexes are partitioned per sponsor cell; object storage uses per-cell prefixes or buckets with cell-scoped credentials; logs and traces carry tenant identifiers and redact personal data. AI features retrieve context only through the governed query layer under the user's tenant context, log retrieved resource identifiers, and never use one tenant's data to train, fine-tune or evaluate models serving another tenant without documented sharing rights. Backups are per cell where the profile allows; for shared-cluster backups the limitations of single-tenant restore are documented and tested. Support and observability tools show tenant-scoped views by default.
intended_practice: Extend the typed tenant context to cache, queue, index and storage clients; partition AI retrieval; document backup limitations.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design extends tenant isolation to caches, queues, search, files, logs, backups and AI features, which retrieve context only under the requesting user's tenant. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Third-party model providers process prompts outside Echelon's isolation boundary; contractual and data-minimization controls apply.
Shared physical backups cannot guarantee independent per-tenant recovery (UNB-TEN-014).

title: Tenant-scoped encryption keys, customer-managed keys and cryptographic erasure
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-006 and UNB-TEN-008 require partner-scoped keys to the degree promised by contract; RR-UNB-TEN-016-r1 requires destruction by tenant-scoped key destruction under dual control and a destruction certificate. The key hierarchy is an open design decision (ADR-006, PARTNER-SEGREGATION pending decisions). Not implemented.
target_answer: Each sponsor cell has its own data encryption keys under a key hierarchy in a managed key service, with sensitive fields additionally encrypted at the application layer under cell-specific keys so that database-level access alone does not reveal them. Customers that require it can supply or hold their own root key; revoking it renders their data unavailable, and the service behavior on revocation is documented. On exit, cell keys are destroyed under dual control after retention and legal-hold checks, and a destruction certificate states what persists (for example immutable backups until expiry) and when. Compromise of one cell's keys does not expose another cell.
intended_practice: Decide the key hierarchy (ADR-006); implement per-cell keys and application-layer encryption for sensitive fields.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design encrypts each sponsor's data under its own keys, can support customer-held root keys, and erases a departing sponsor's data by destroying its keys under dual control with a destruction certificate. The key design is not yet decided or built.
residual_risks: Per-tenant keys do not protect against an application-layer flaw that decrypts on behalf of the wrong tenant; they protect storage and backup exposure.
Cryptographic erasure depends on no unencrypted copies existing elsewhere.

challenge.customer_intent: Limit exposure of our data to our own keys and be able to prove deletion.
challenge.adverse_outcome: A storage or backup compromise exposes all tenants; deletion on exit cannot be demonstrated.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Provider-default encryption at rest uses keys shared across tenants and protects only against physical media loss; it does nothing for logical cross-tenant access.
challenge.legally_required: No statute requires per-tenant keys; encryption is addressed in the FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR 314.4(c)(3)) and NYDFS 500.15 for covered entities.
challenge.contractually_required: Large banks increasingly request customer-managed keys.
challenge.historical_convention: Encryption at rest with provider-managed keys.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Deletion uncertainty is largely eliminated by cryptographic erasure if all copies are encrypted under the cell key.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Key service policies; application-layer encryption library.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Key service audit logs; destruction certificates.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Per-cell keys plus application-layer field encryption plus cryptographic erasure.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Partially; key configuration and logs are inspectable, but absence of unencrypted copies is hard to prove.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely valued; customer-held keys may be requested by large banks and declined by small sponsors because of operational burden.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Unencrypted copies in logs, caches, exports or AI artifacts.
challenge.alternative_cost: Moderate to high; key management operations and performance cost of application-layer encryption.
challenge.alternative_risks: Key loss causes data loss; customer key revocation can cause outages affecting fiduciary obligations.
opposing_arguments: Per-tenant keys are often oversold as isolation; they do not stop logical cross-tenant access through the application.

title: Noisy neighbor and per-tenant resource isolation
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-015 requires partner-specific performance, availability, recovery and capacity targets and noisy-neighbor detection and isolation in shared tiers. The persistence design test matrix includes a ten-times surge and noisy-neighbor test per profile. UNB-TEN-018 requires benchmarking before engine selection. PARTNER-SEGREGATION scenario 8 requires a failed migration for one partner not to affect others. Not implemented.
target_answer: Each tenant has rate limits, query timeouts, connection pool quotas and job concurrency limits enforced at the API gateway, connection broker and job scheduler. Time-critical work (grant disbursement windows, year-end receipting) runs in priority queues with per-tenant fairness so one tenant's surge cannot delay another's deadlines. Per-tenant latency and error rates are monitored with alerts on cross-tenant contention. Schema migrations are applied per cell with independent failure handling, so one cell's failed migration leaves others unaffected. Tenants whose load or contract requires it move to a dedicated profile without changing identifiers.
intended_practice: Benchmark per UNB-TEN-018; implement quotas and per-cell migration.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design applies per-tenant rate limits and quotas, prioritizes time-critical work fairly across tenants, and migrates each sponsor's schema independently so one failure does not affect others. This is designed, not built or benchmarked.
residual_risks: Shared database engine resources (locks, WAL, autovacuum, replication) can still couple tenants on one cluster.

title: White-label, embedded and distribution-partner isolation and partner exit
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-020 distinguishes sponsor, distribution partner, channel and DAF account; UNB-TEN-010 prevents partner preferences overriding sponsor authority; RR-UNB-TEN-016-r1 states distribution partners receive only data the sponsor authorizes; AIN-029 requires embeds to independently authorize, expire and not impersonate the sponsor; CNV-PLT-001 makes the sponsor the sender in white-label programs; UNB-XIN-SAS-007 governs partner exit. Not implemented.
target_answer: Distribution partners are typed partitions inside the sponsor cell. A partner's users, APIs and widgets can reach only donors and funds in that partner's channel and only the data classes the sponsor authorizes for that partner; cross-partner movement of a donor or fund requires an approved transfer, never a data copy. Embedded components run in an isolated origin with scoped tokens and cannot be scripted by the host page. Branding, templates and sender identity are versioned per program and validated so a communication cannot be sent under another partner's brand. On partner exit, partner access, API clients and subscriptions end at the effective time, donors retain access through pre-provisioned sponsor-direct credentials, and the exit case reconciles every fund.
intended_practice: Implement partner partitions with the same typed context and RLS policies as programs; implement the PartnerExit case.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design confines each distribution partner and white-label channel to the donors and data the sponsor authorizes, isolates embedded components from host pages, prevents cross-brand messages, and ends partner access cleanly at exit while donors keep access. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Partners hold copies of data the sponsor authorized; protection of those copies is the partner's responsibility.

title: Tenant lifecycle: provisioning, profile migration, export and offboarding evidence
status_rationale: RR-UNB-TEN-011-r1 defines a TenantLifecycle state machine including ReadinessValidated; UNB-TEN-012 and UNB-TEN-013 govern migration between profiles with a high-water mark, record equivalence, independent reconciliation and single-writer fencing; RR-UNB-TEN-016-r1 requires an ExitPackage within 30 days with a signed manifest and trial balances; UNB-TEN-017 records the isolation profile in effect over time. Not implemented.
target_answer: Tenants move through a governed lifecycle state machine. Go-live requires a ReadinessValidated state that includes passing the isolation test matrix for that tenant's profile. Migration between profiles uses a consistent event high-water mark, record-by-record equivalence verification, independent ledger reconciliation and fencing so there is never more than one authoritative writer, and preserves all identifiers and history. On exit, the sponsor receives within 30 days an ExitPackage with full event history, projections, documents, policies, audit records and a signed manifest with digests, counts and reconciled trial balances that it can verify independently; the tenant then enters read-only retention before key destruction. The profile and controls in effect at any past time are queryable.
intended_practice: Implement the lifecycle state machine with isolation readiness checks and the export package.
customer_statement: Echelon's Unbound design moves each tenant through a governed lifecycle that requires isolation tests before go-live, preserves history across migrations with a single authoritative writer, and delivers a verifiable signed export within 30 days of exit. This is designed, not built.
residual_risks: Migration is a high-risk window; interrupted cutover scenarios (PARTNER-SEGREGATION scenario 6) must be tested.
